claims.text: A thin titanium interlayer in HEA multilayers will promote a transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
A titanium interlayer will enhance coherency between adjacent HEA layers.
HEA multilayers without a transition layer have less-coherent interfaces.
Less-coherent interfaces favor diffusion-mediated creep at lower stresses and intermediate temperatures.
A thin titanium interlayer can be deposited between HEA layers by magnetron sputtering.
Titanium has an intermediate lattice parameter capable of bridging the lattice mismatch between the adjacent HEA layers.
Reducing lattice mismatch through the titanium interlayer will improve interface coherency.
Lattice misfit and coherent interfaces can affect high-temperature deformation behavior in HEAs.
Improved interface coherency will reduce the driving force for rapid atomic diffusion along the interface.
The coherent titanium-containing interface will continue to permit dislocation motion under applied stress.
Suppressing interfacial diffusion will promote dislocation-mediated creep.
A titanium interlayer will decrease diffusion-dominated creep rates.
A titanium interlayer will increase the prominence of dislocation-mediated creep.
The creep-mechanism shift will be observable through a change in stress exponent and dislocation morphology.
The titanium interlayer will produce a higher yield strength during creep testing.
HEA multilayers without an interlayer predominantly exhibit diffusion-mediated creep under the proposed testing conditions.
The proposed effect is limited to a moderate temperature and stress window in which interface coherency dominates creep.
At very high temperatures or extreme stresses, grain-boundary sliding or void formation may override the titanium interlayer's influence.
The optimal titanium-interlayer thickness and composition are unknown.
A controlled comparison of multilayers with and without titanium interlayers can test the proposed creep-mechanism shift.
